NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING 
FIRST MID SESSIONAL — EXTENDED MODEL ANSWER SHEET

Q.1 (a) Text Preprocessing and Normalization 
Text preprocessing is the process of converting raw, unstructured text into a clean and standardized form that can be 
understood and processed by an NLP system. It reduces noise and makes important linguistic information easier for 
algorithms to learn. The major steps are: 
1. Tokenization 
Tokenization divides a sentence or document into smaller units called tokens. Tokens may be words, punctuation marks, 
or subwords. For example, the sentence “The students are studying NLP.” can be tokenized as [The, students, are, 
studying, NLP, .]. Tokenization is the basic step used before most NLP operations. 
2. Stop-word Removal 
Stop words are very common words such as “the”, “is”, “are”, “a”, “an”, “of", and “to”. They often carry little information for 
tasks such as document classification. Removing them reduces the number of features. For example, “The boy is playing 
in the park” may become “boy playing park”. However, stop-word removal should be used carefully because words such as 
“not” can be important for sentiment analysis. 
3. Stemming 
Stemming reduces related words to a common stem by applying simple rules, often by removing prefixes or suffixes. For 
example, “playing”, “played”, and “plays” may be reduced to “play”. Stemming is fast but the resulting stem may not always 
be a valid dictionary word; for example, “studies” may become “studi” with some stemmers. 
4. Lemmatization 
Lemmatization converts a word to its meaningful dictionary base form, called a lemma, using vocabulary and grammatical 
information. For example, “studies” becomes “study”, “better” may be mapped to “good” depending on the linguistic 
resources, and “running” becomes “run. It is generally more linguistically accurate than stemming but can be slower. 
Conclusion: Example of complete preprocessing: Raw sentence: “The students are studying Natural Language 
Processing!” After tokenization: [The, students, are, studying, Natural, Language, Processing, !] After stop-word removal: 
[students, studying, Natural, Language, Processing] After stemming: [student, studi, natur, languag, process] After 
lemmatization: [student, study, Natural, Language, Processing] Thus, preprocessing and normalization improve 
consistency, reduce unnecessary vocabulary, and prepare text for tasks such as classification, sentiment analysis, 
information retrieval, and machine translation.

Q.1 (b) Concept of Text Preprocessing 
Text preprocessing is the preparation of raw text before it is supplied to an NLP algorithm. Real-world text may contain 
punctuation, unnecessary spaces, spelling variations, numbers, symbols, URLs, stop words, and different forms of the 
same word. Preprocessing converts this noisy input into a useful representation. 
Important preprocessing operations 
Common operations include: 
« Cleaning unwanted characters, HTML tags, URLs, and exira spaces. 
« Converting text to a consistent case, usually lowercase. 
« Tokenization into words or subwords. 
« Stop-word removal when appropriate. 
« Stemming or lemmatization to normalize word forms. 
« Handling punctuation, numbers, emojis, and special symbols according to the application. 
« Converting the cleaned text into numerical features such as Bag-of-Words or TF-IDF. 
Example 
Consider: “NLP is AMAZING!!! NLP helps computers understand human language.” A basic preprocessing pipeline may 
produce: “nlp amazing nlp helps computers understand human language”. It can then be tokenized into individual words 
and represented numerically for machine learning. 
Importance 
Preprocessing reduces noise, decreases vocabulary size, improves computational efficiency, and can improve model 
performance. The exact operations should depend on the NLP task; aggressive preprocessing may remove useful 
information in applications such as sentiment analysis or named entity recognition. 
Conclusion: In short, text preprocessing creates a standardized input representation from raw language. Itis an essential 
first stage in many NLP pipelines because machine-learning models generally work better when irrelevant variation and 
noise are controlled.

Q.2 (a) Natural Language Processing: Scope and Applications 
Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of Artificial Intelligence, computer science, and linguistics concerned with 
enabling computers to process, understand, interpret, and generate human language. NLP deals with both written and 
spoken language. 
Scope of NLP 
The scope of NLP includes: 
1. Text preprocessing and normalization. 
. Morphological and syntactic analysis such as part-of-speech tagging and parsing. 
. Semantic analysis and word-sense understanding. 
. Information extraction and named entity recognition. 
. Text classification and sentiment analysis. 
. Question answering and conversational systems. 
. Machine translation. 
. Speech recognition and language generation. 
. Text summarization and information retrieval. 
a4 0 o N 
oA ® N 
. Machine Translation 
Machine translation automatically converts text from one language to another. For example, an English sentence can be 
translated into Hindi or Marathi. Modern systems use neural networks and contextual representations to improve fluency 
and meaning preservation. 
2. Sentiment Analysis 
Sentiment analysis identifies the opinion or emotional polarity expressed in text, such as positive, negative, or neutral. It is 
used for product reviews, social-media monitoring, customer feedback, and market research. 
3. Chatbots 
NLP enables chatbots to understand user questions and generate suitable responses. Applications include customer 
support, educational assistants, banking helpdesks, and service portals. Intent detection and entity extraction are 
commonly used in such systems. 
4. Speech Recognition 
Speech recognition converts spoken language into text. It is used in voice assistants, dictation systems, call-center 
analytics, and accessibility tools. The system must handle pronunciation, accents, background noise, and context. 
Conclusion: Therefore, NLP connects human communication with computer systems. Its applications improve 
automation, search, communication, accessibility, and decision support across many industries.

Q.2 (b) Linguistics 
Linguistics is the scientific study of human language. It examines how language is structured, how meaning is created, how 
sounds are produced, and how language is used in society. Linguistics is an important foundation of NLP because 
computers need linguistic knowledge to process human language effectively. 
Major areas of linguistics 
1. Phonetics: studies the physical production and perception of speech sounds. 
2. Phonology: studies how sounds are organized and function within a language. 
3. Morphology: studies the internal structure of words and morphemes. For example, “unhappiness” contains meaningful 
", “happy”, and “ness”. 
parts such as “un-", 
4. Syntax: studies how words combine to form grammatical sentences. 
5. Semantics: studies literal meaning of words, phrases, and sentences. 
6. Pragmatics: studies meaning in context and how speakers convey intended meaning. 
7. Discourse: studies relationships between sentences and larger units of communication. 
Linguistics in NLP 
Linguistic knowledge supports tasks such as tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, parsing, semantic analysis, machine 
translation, speech processing, and information extraction. For example, syntax helps a system identify the grammatical 
relationship between “student” and “reads” in “The student reads a book.” Semantics helps distinguish meanings of 
ambiguous words using context. 
Example 
The word “unhappiness” can be analyzed morphologically as un + happy + ness. In the sentence “The student opened the 
book,” syntax identifies the subject, verb, and object, while semantics helps interpret their roles. 
Conclusion: Thus, linguistics provides the theoretical understanding of language, while NLP uses computational methods 
to implement language processing on computers. Both fields complement each other in building effective language 
technologies.

Q.3 (a) Text Categorization 
Text categorization, also called text classification, is the process of assigning a document or text to one or more predefined 
categories. It is a supervised machine-learning task in which a model learns from labeled examples and predicts the 
category of unseen text. 
Basic steps 
1. Collect labeled documents, such as emails labeled Spam or Not Spam. 
. Preprocess the text using tokenization, normalization, and other suitable techniques. 
. Convert text into numerical features using Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF, or embeddings. 
2 
3 
4. Split data into training and testing sets. 
5. Train a classifier such as Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, or SVM. 
6. Predict categories for new documents. 
7. Evaluate the model using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, or a confusion matrix. 
Example 
Suppose an email classifier has two classes: Spam and Ham. Training examples containing terms such as “free”, “offer”, 
and “winner” may be associated with Spam, while ordinary messages about classes or meetings may be associated with 
Ham. For a new email, the trained model calculates the likelihood of each class and assigns the most suitable label. 
Applications 
Text categorization is used in spam detection, news classification, sentiment classification, topic labeling, 
customer-support routing, document organization, and toxic-content detection. 
Advantages and challenges 
It can automatically organize large collections of documents and reduce manual effort. Challenges include class 
imbalance, ambiguous language, domain-specific vocabulary, sarcasm, spelling variations, and changes in language over 
time. 
Conclusion: Hence, text categorization converts unstructured language into useful predefined labels. The quality of 
preprocessing, feature representation, training data, and classifier all affect the final classification performance.

Q.3 (b) Various N-gram Models 
An n-gram is a contiguous sequence of n words or tokens in a text. N-gram language models estimate the probability of a 
word based on a limited history of previous words. They are useful in language modeling, spelling correction, 
autocomplete, speech recognition, and other NLP tasks. 
1. Unigram model 
A unigram model considers one word at a time and assumes words are independent. For a sentence containing w1, w2, 
..., wn, the probability is approximated as the product of individual word probabilities. Example tokens: “I", “like”, “NLP" are 
treated independently. 
2. Bigram model 
A bigram contains two consecutive words. It estimates P(wi | wi-1). For “I like NLP", the bigrams are “I like” and “like NLP". 
Bigrams capture immediate word-to-word relationships better than unigrams. 
3. Trigram model 
A trigram contains three consecutive words and estimates P(wi | wi-2, wi-1). For “I like studying NLP”", examples include “I 
like studying” and “like studying NLP". It uses more context than a bigram. 
4. Higher-order n-grams 
4-gram, 5-gram, and larger models use longer contexts. They can capture more local context but require more training 
data and have a greater risk of unseen combinations and data sparsity. 
Probability and smoothing 
The general chain approximation is P(w1...wn) = [T P(wi | previous n—1 words). Because many possible n-grams may 
never occur in training data, smoothing methods such as Laplace/add-one smoothing can assign non-zero probability to 
unseen n-grams. Larger n usually gives more context but increases computational and data requirements. 
Conclusion: Example: Sentence: I love natural language processing.” Unigrams: | 
| love | natural | language | processing 
Bigrams: | love | love natural | natural language | language processing Trigrams: | love natural | love natural language | 
natural language processing Thus, n-gram models provide a simple statistical way to model local word sequences. 
Although neural language models are widely used today, n-grams remain important for understanding the fundamentals of 
language modeling.

Q.4 (a) Naive Bayes Algorithm for Text Classification 
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic supervised-learning algorithm widely used for text classification. It is based on Bayes’ 
theorem and makes a simplifying assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class. Despite this 
assumption, it often performs well for high-dimensional text data. 
Bayes’ theorem 
P(CID) = [P(DIC) P(C)1/ P(D) 
where C is a class and D is a document. For a document containing words w1, w2, ..., wn, the Naive Bayes approximation 
is: 
P(CID) = P(C) x IT Pwi|C) 
The predicted class is the class with the highest posterior score. 
Working steps 
1. Collect labeled training documents. 
2. Calculate the prior probability P(C) for each class. 
3. Calculate word probabilities P(w|C) from the training documents. 
4. Apply smoothing, commonly Laplace smoothing, so unseen words do not produce zero probability. 
5. For a new document, multiply the class prior by the word likelihoods. 
6. Assign the document to the class with the highest posterior score. 
Worked example 
Suppose there are two classes: Sports and Technology. Assume a small training set gives: 
P(Sports)=0.6, P(Technology)=0.4. 
For the words “team” and “software”, suppose after Laplace smoothing: 
P(team|Sports)=0.20, P(software|Sports)=0.05 
P(team|Technology)=0.05, P(software|Technology)=0.20 
For D = “team software”: 
Sports score = 0.6 x 0.20 x 0.05 = 0.006 
Technology score = 0.4 x 0.05 x 0.20 = 0.004 
Since 0.006 > 0.004, the document is classified as Sports. These values are unnormalized scores; normalization is 
unnecessary when only the winning class is required. 
Advantages 
Naive Bayes is simple, fast, memory-efficient, easy to implement, and effective for sparse high-dimensional text. It works 
well even with relatively small training datasets. 
Limitations 
The conditional-independence assumption is often unrealistic because words are related to one another. Performance can 
decrease when word order and complex interactions are important. Zero-frequency problems must also be handled with 
smoothing. 
Conclusion: Naive Bayes is especially useful as a strong baseline for spam detection, topic classification, sentiment 
analysis, and document classification because text data usually contains many sparse features.

Q.4 (b) Decision Tree vs Support Vector Machine 
Decision Tree and Support Vector Machine (SVM) are supervised-learning algorithms that can be used for text 
classification. Their working principles are different, and each has particular advantages and limitations. 
Decision Tree — working principle 
A Decision Tree recursively splits the training data using feature-based rules. Each internal node represents a decision on 
a feature, branches represent outcomes, and leaf nodes represent class labels. Splits are commonly selected using 
measures such as Gini impurity or information gain. For text classification, features may be word counts or TF-IDF values. 
SVM - working principle 
SVM finds a decision boundary, or hyperplane, that separates classes while maximizing the margin between the classes. 
The most informative training examples near the boundary are called support vectors. Kernels can be used when a 
nonlinear boundary is required, although linear SVM is particularly effective for high-dimensional sparse text. 
Comparison 
Decision Tree: 
« Easy to understand and visualize. 
« Produces rule-based decisions. 
« Requires relatively little feature scaling. 
« Can overfit unless depth and other parameters are controlled. 
« May be less effective than linear SVM on very high-dimensional sparse text. 
SVM: 
« Strong performance in high-dimensional spaces. 
« Linear SVM works very well with sparse TF-IDF features. 
« Good generalization with an appropriate margin and regularization. 
« Less interpretable than a small Decision Tree. 
« Training can be more computationally demanding for very large datasets, depending on implementation. 
Suitability for text data 
Text classification commonly produces thousands or millions of sparse features. Linear SVM is often highly suitable 
because it can learn an effective separating hyperplane in high-dimensional space. Decision Trees can still be useful when 
interpretability and rule-based explanations are important, but a single tree may struggle with extremely large sparse 
vocabularies. 
Conclusion: Conclusion: If interpretability and simple decision rules are the priority, a Decision Tree is attractive. If the 
main goal is strong classification performance on high-dimensional sparse text such as TF-IDF vectors, SVM—especially a 
linear SVM—is generally a more suitable choice.
